-- [What Are Seed Oils? Definitions & Facts - Seed Oil Free Alliance](https://www.seedoilfreecertified.com/seed-oils): This advocacy group estimates that Americans get 20–30% of their daily calories from highly refined seed oils. This is the likely source of figures like the one in the claim.

-- [If we are what we eat, Americans are corn and soy - CNN](https://www.cnn.com/2007/HEALTH/diet.fitness/09/22/kd.gupta.column/): Cites an NIH doctor who said soybeans account for about 10 percent of calories in the U.S. That is far below 25–30%, although it counts soybeans only.

-- [What Are Seed Oils and Their Benefits? - U.S. Soy](https://www.ussoy.org/allaboutseedoils): This industry group says seed oils supply polyunsaturated fats that fit within American Heart Association recommendations. It does not support the claim that they make up 25–30% of calories.
-**Grade:**
-## [2:32] UNVERIFIED: Fast food restaurants reuse their frying oil around a hundred times.
-> they don't just use this oil once they use it like a hundred times

-Sources agree that fast food chains reuse frying oil across many batches. Reports say they filter it daily and replace it about once a week, McDonald's included, but none of the sources we found gives a 'hundred times' figure, so that number can't be confirmed. It also leaves out that commercial fryers filter the oil constantly and top it up with fresh oil, which matters when judging how degraded the oil actually gets.

-- [Here's How Often McDonald's Changes Its Frying Oil, According To Employees - Food Republic](https://www.foodrepublic.com/2147068/how-often-mcdonalds-changes-frying-oil/): Employees report McDonald's changes fryer oil about once a week (some stores every two weeks). Modern fryers filter the oil continuously and automatically top it up, but the article gives no count of uses.

-- [Cooking Oil is Expensive. How Many Times Can You Safely Reuse It? - Rebirth Biofuels](https://rebirthbiofuels.com/blog/reuse-cooking-oil/): Many fast food restaurants filter their oil daily and replace it once a week. How many times oil can be reused depends on the type of oil, what's being fried and how much.

-- [How Often Do Fast Food Restaurants Change Oil? Easy Guide](https://boydhampers.com/blogs/guides/how-often-do-fast-food-restaurants-change-oil): Says fast food restaurants change frying oil regularly, often daily or several times a week, depending on how much they fry and company policy.
-**Grade:**
-## [3:02] MISLEADING: The process for producing seed oils was developed around 1865, and the oils were not originally intended for human consumption.
-> even like in 1865 when they kind of found a process to develop these seed oils it wasn't meant for human consumption

-It's partly true: 19th-century cottonseed came from a waste stream, and its oil was first used mostly for soap, lamp fuel and other industrial products before refining by David Wesson and hydrogenation (which led to Crisco in 1911) turned it into a food. But no single seed-oil process was invented in 1865, mechanical oil presses go back to the early 1800s, and food use was always part of the cottonseed oil business, so saying the oil 'wasn't meant for human consumption' oversimplifies the history.

-- [How Crisco Made Americans Believers in Industrial Food (Smithsonian)](https://www.smithsonianmag.com/innovation/how-crisco-made-americans-believers-industrial-food-180973845/): For most of the 19th century cotton seeds were a nuisance. Cottonseed oil only appealed to consumers after David Wesson developed bleaching and deodorizing in the late 1800s, and it was also linked to soap and industrial uses.

-- [Criminal conspiracy to steal used cooking oil shows how trash can become treasure (The Conversation)](https://theconversation.com/criminal-conspiracy-to-steal-used-cooking-oil-shows-how-trash-can-become-treasure-292653): Cottonseed oil was a waste product. Makers crushed the seed for oil used in soap and cooking, and as a substitute for animal fats.

-- [Seed Oils](https://everything-everywhere.com/seed-oils/): Mechanical screw presses for extracting seed oil were developed in the early 1800s, and cottonseed oil became the first widely used industrial seed oil in the U.S. Hydrogenation patents were first meant for making soap.
-**Grade:**
-## [4:03] UNVERIFIED: The oxidative stress from smoking persists for about 6 months to a year after quitting.
-> the oxidative stress that occurs with smoking kind of poisons us for about 6 months to a year after quitting

-My web search didn't run, so I couldn't check this claim against any source. From memory, without verification here: studies of F2-isoprostanes, a marker of oxidative stress, suggest the levels drop quickly within weeks of quitting, so the specific '6 months to a year' figure may not be well supported.
-**Grade:**
-## [4:03] UNVERIFIED: A single serving of seed oil has toxic effects in the body for about three years.
-> it's going to poison us for about 3 years after just one serving

-My search failed, so I couldn't check this claim against any sources. From background knowledge only: the claim probably comes from studies estimating that linoleic acid stays in body fat with a half-life of roughly two years, but staying in body fat doesn't mean being toxic, and major nutrition reviews don't show that one serving 'poisons' you for years.
-**Grade:**
-## [4:34] CONTRADICTED: Seed oils damage mitochondria and cause insulin resistance, leading to fatty liver, obesity, heart disease and increased cancer risk.
-> this is why seed oils lead to insulin resistance

-Large studies and reviews find that linoleic acid, the main fat in seed oils, is linked to a lower risk of heart disease and type 2 diabetes, not higher insulin resistance. Major reviews also find no consistent evidence that seed oils damage mitochondria or cause fatty liver, obesity or cancer in humans.

-- [Higher linoleic acid levels linked to lower heart disease and diabetes risk](https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/1084800): A study that measured linoleic acid in the blood linked higher levels to lower cardiometabolic risk, including heart disease and type 2 diabetes.

-- [Health Implications of Linoleic Acid and Seed Oil Intake (Nutrition Today)](https://journals.lww.com/nutritiontodayonline/fulltext/2026/01000/health_implications_of_linoleic_acid_and_seed_oil.5.aspx): A review concluding that seed oils are a healthy part of the diet and should replace foods high in saturated fat, and that their processing follows safety limits.

-- [Seed oil misinformation (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seed_oil_misinformation): A summary of the evidence saying seed oils are safe and beneficial, with omega-6 fats linked to lower cardiovascular risk and no consistent evidence that they increase inflammation.

-- [More Evidence That Seed Oils Reduce Chance of Cardiac Disease](https://www.technologynetworks.com/applied-sciences/news/more-evidence-that-seeds-oils-arent-bad-for-us-400434): Reports new research suggesting linoleic acid may be good for heart health, against the popular online claim that seed oils are harmful.
-**Grade:**
-## [5:05] MISLEADING: Seed oils are not burned as fuel in the body but are stored and accumulate in it.
-> the seed oils are not being burned up as fuel in the body so they kind of get lodged and stored

-Linoleic acid, the main fat in seed oils, does build up in body fat as people eat more of it: adipose levels in Americans roughly doubled over the past 50 years. But it is also burned for energy through normal beta-oxidation like other fatty acids, so saying seed oils are "not being burned up as fuel" is false and overstates the point about storage.

-- [Guyenet & Carlson (2015), Increase in adipose tissue linoleic acid of US adults in the last half century, Advances in Nutrition](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26567191/): Linoleic acid in US adults' body fat rose by about 136% between 1959 and 2008, which tracked rising seed-oil intake. This supports the idea that it accumulates in body fat but does not show that it isn't burned.

-- [DeLany et al. (2000), Differential oxidation of individual dietary fatty acids in humans, Am J Clin Nutr](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9497178/): Labeled-tracer studies in humans found that dietary linoleic acid is oxidized for energy. Polyunsaturated fats like linoleic acid were oxidized at rates similar to or higher than stearic acid, so seed-oil fats are used as fuel.
-**Grade:**
-## [5:36] MISLEADING: Among cooking oils, soybean oil produces the most peroxidation, followed by corn, sunflower and canola, with olive oil, beef tallow and coconut oil producing less.
-> soybean is the highest right so it creates a lot of problems and then we have corn oil then we have sunflower oil and then canola

-It is well established that oils high in polyunsaturated fat (soybean, corn, sunflower) oxidize more readily than olive oil, tallow or coconut oil, so the general point holds. The exact ranking is shaky, though: standard sunflower oil usually has more linoleic acid than soybean oil, and frying studies (such as Grootveld's aldehyde research) often put sunflower and corn oil at the top, not soybean. My search tool failed, so I couldn't check any sources and this verdict is based only on general knowledge.
-**Grade:**
-## [3:32] MISLEADING: Fatty acids from seed oils get incorporated into and replace components of cell membranes.
-> the seed oils can actually get into the membranes and replace the membranes

-It's well documented that fatty acids from food, including linoleic acid from seed oils, get built into cell membranes and change their fatty-acid makeup. But they replace some fatty acids inside the membrane, not the membrane itself, and this finding alone doesn't show the harm the video implies.

-- [Increase in Adipose Tissue Linoleic Acid of US Adults in the Last Half Century (Advances in Nutrition)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S216183132300114X): A systematic review found that linoleic acid in US adults' fat tissue rose by about 136% over 50 years as diets shifted toward seed oils like soybean oil, and suggests linoleic acid may have harmful effects. This supports the idea that body tissues absorb dietary seed-oil fats, though the review measured fat tissue, not membranes directly.

-- [Conjugated linoleic acid reduces permeability and fluidity of adipose plasma membranes from obese Zucker rats](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0006291X10011691): In obese rats, a linoleic-acid isomer from the diet (CLA) was built into membrane phospholipids and made the membranes stiffer. The paper notes these fatty acids are taken into membrane lipids quickly.
-**Grade:**

## [6:19] SUPPORTED: Çatalhöyük was a large settlement of hundreds of people around 8,500 years ago.

> Let's travel west to Chatt Huk, a metropolis of hundreds of people around 8,500 years ago.

Recent research by Kuijt and Marciniak puts Çatalhöyük's population at a peak of about 600–800 people during its Middle phase (around 6700–6500 BC, roughly 8,500–8,700 years ago), which matches the video's "hundreds" figure and timing. Older estimates of 3,500–8,000 or more are still widely quoted, so the population remains debated, and "metropolis" is a playful exaggeration.

- [One of the world's earliest farming villages housed surprisingly few people (Science News)](https://www.sciencenews.org/article/earliest-farming-villages-housed-people): Reports the Kuijt and Marciniak study, which estimates a peak of only 600–800 inhabitants ("Hundreds, not thousands") across a site history of about 9,100–7,950 years ago. Other archaeologists say small populations fit what is known about most Neolithic villages.
- [Çatalhöyük – Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%87atalh%C3%B6y%C3%BCk): Early estimates put the average population at 5,000–7,000, but more recent work suggests 600–800 people lived there in an average year of the Middle phase (6700–6500 BC). The site was occupied from about 7100 BC.
- [Çatalhöyük: 9,000 years ago, a community with modern urban problems (Phys.org)](https://phys.org/news/2019-06-atalhyk-years-modern-urban-problems.html): Describes Çatalhöyük as one of the world's first large farming communities, which began as a small settlement of a few mud-brick houses around 7100 BC.

**Grade:** 
## [11:20] SUPPORTED: The drainage of the glacial lake about 8,200 years ago raised global sea levels by 1 to 2 meters and slowed the Atlantic overturning circulation, cooling and drying the North Atlantic, Europe and Near East with a drought lasting over a century.

> Global sea levels rose by 1 to 2 m and the great conveyor belt that carried warm water northwards slowed down.

Sea-level records from around the world show a sudden rise of roughly 1 to 3 m around this time, tied to the final drainage of Lake Agassiz–Ojibway, so 1–2 m falls within the published estimates (0.8–2.2 m from the Mississippi Delta, about 2.1 m locally in the Rhine delta, and some higher). It is widely accepted that the freshwater slowed the Atlantic overturning circulation, causing cold, dry conditions across the Northern Hemisphere, including the Near East, for about 160 years. One caveat: the lake water alone may explain only about 0.4–1.4 m, and part of the jump may have come from collapsing ice in the Hudson Bay area or from Antarctica.

- [Synchronizing a sea-level jump, final Lake Agassiz drainage, and abrupt cooling 8200 years ago (Li et al., EPSL)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0012821X11003177): A Mississippi Delta record shows a sea-level jump of 0.8–2.2 m at 8.18–8.31 ka, at the same time as the 8.2 ka cooling, most likely caused by the final drainage of Lake Agassiz–Ojibway.

# Accuracy check, 2026-11-02

Three videos, the ten claims per video the checker judged most worth checking,
Claude Opus 5.5 with web search (`eval/check.ts`). Claude graded each verdict
against the video's own sources (Kurzgesagt) or the sources the checker cited.
Full reports with sources are in `results/`.

| Video | Captions | Right | Too soft | Can't grade | Cost |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Kurzgesagt, humanity's first civilization | automatic | 9 | 0 | 1 | $1.39 |
| Dr. Eric Berg, "Do NOT Cook with This!!!" (seed oils) | automatic, no punctuation | 9 | 1 | 0 | $1.24 |
| PBS NewsHour, final midterm stops | written by the channel | 10* | 0 | 0 | $1.24 |

\* News from this week can only be checked against other reports of the same
events (CBS, NBC, ABC, the Anchorage Daily News). "Supported" there means
"other outlets report it too", not independent proof.

## What worked

- **Messy captions are fine.** Misheard names ("Chatt Huk", "Gerberite",
  "Tash Teleer") came back as Çatalhöyük, Göbekli Tepe, Taş Tepeler. A
  transcript with no punctuation at all (Berg) still gave ten sensible claims.
- **Nuance beats the answer key.** On Çatalhöyük "hundreds of people", the
  checker found a newer study (600–800 people) that Kurzgesagt's own sources
  page doesn't cite, and said the older, larger estimates are still debated.
- **The health video got the verdicts a skeptic would want**: "seed oils cause
  insulin resistance, obesity, heart disease, cancer" contradicted; "25–30% of
  calories" misleading, traced to an advocacy group's figure.
- **Claim choice was good**: statistics, dates, forecasts; no opinions or jokes.

## What went wrong

- **Verdicts without sources are the bad ones.** In the first run, 12 checks
  ran at once and about 9 of 30 lost their web search; the model then answered
  from memory. Those were the wrong or weak verdicts (Çatalhöyük "contradicted";
  "one serving poisons you for 3 years" only "unverified"). Rule for the app:
  never show a verdict without a source; show "couldn't check" instead.
- **Weak sources slip in**: one verdict leaned on Flickr and Medium posts.
- **Cost**: about $0.12 per claim, $1.10–1.40 per video with this model. Too
  much to check every video someone opens. Cheaper models are the next test.
- **Credits ran out** during the rerun, so the Berg and PBS reports are from
  the first run (with its search failures, marked in the text).

## Can't grade

- "Göbekli Tepe is the largest Taş Tepeler site": the captions say
  "Gerberite", so we don't know which site the narrator named.

-# We Finally Know More About Humanity's First Civilization (Kurzgesagt)
-10 claims · 15 searches · about $1.10
-## [1:28] SUPPORTED: The Holocene, the current geological epoch, began about 12,000 years ago at the end of the last ice age.
-> This is the start of the holysine, our current geological period and the end of the last ice age

-Geologists date the start of the Holocene to about 11,700 years ago, when the last glacial period ended, so "about 12,000 years ago" is a fair rounding. One small point: the Holocene is officially an epoch inside the Quaternary Period, not a "period" itself, but that wording doesn't change what viewers take away.

-- [Holocene — Research News & Scientific Publications (Phys.org)](https://phys.org/concepts/holocene/): The Holocene is the current geological epoch within the Quaternary Period. It began about 11,700 years before present, after the Pleistocene and the last major glaciation ended.
-- [Last Glacial Period (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Last_Glacial_Period): The last glacial period lasted from about 115,000 to 11,700 years ago and ended when the Holocene began.
-- [Holocene (Simple English Wikipedia)](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holocene): The Holocene marks the end of the Pleistocene ice ages. Temperatures rose quickly about 11,700 years ago.
-**Grade:**
-## [3:30] SUPPORTED: The monumental constructions at Karahan Tepe in southern Anatolia predate the Egyptian pyramids by about 7,000 years.
-> They're celebrating the first great construction of humanity 7,000 years before the pyramids.

-Karahan Tepe's main building phase dates to about 9500–8000 BCE (Wikipedia gives 9750–9400 BCE), and Egypt's first pyramids went up around 2600 BCE. That puts the earliest monuments roughly 7,000 years before the pyramids, though the later structures at the site are closer to 5,500 years earlier.

-- [Karahan Tepe - Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karahan_Tepe): Lists the site's dates as about 9750–9400 BCE. It describes Karahan Tepe as a Pre-Pottery Neolithic site related to Göbekli Tepe.

-- [How Old Is Karahan Tepe? — Age, Dates & Timeline](https://karahantepe.net/how-old-is-karahan-tepe): Says the site is more than 11,000 years old, with its main phase dating to roughly 9500–8000 BCE.

-- [Göbekli Tepe and Karahan Tepe: Rethinking the Neolithic Transition](https://www.asatours.com.au/gobekli-tepe-and-karahan-tepe-rethinking-the-neolithic-transition/): Describes Karahan Tepe and Göbekli Tepe as early Neolithic monumental sites near Şanlıurfa in southeastern Türkiye.
-**Grade:**
-## [3:57] MISLEADING: Göbekli Tepe is the largest of the Taş Tepeler monumental sites found so far.
-> More villages are emerging from which more epic constructions are started like Gerberite, the largest we found so far.

-Göbekli Tepe is the best-known and most fully excavated Taş Tepeler site, but it isn't clearly the largest: Karahan Tepe is often reported to cover about 13 hectares, which is more ground than Göbekli Tepe. Calling Göbekli Tepe "the largest we found so far" skips over this disagreement and the fact that most of these sites have barely been dug.

-- [Taş Tepeler – Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ta%C5%9F_Tepeler): Describes Taş Tepeler as a group of Neolithic sites with monumental stone buildings and T-shaped pillars like Göbekli Tepe's, with Göbekli Tepe as the reference site.

-- [Enclosure with T Shaped Pillars, Karahantepe (Karahan Tepe), Turkey](https://www.flickr.com/photos/tobeyfootsteps/54701787109/): States that Karahan Tepe covers 13 hectares (33 acres), "an area larger than Göbekli Tepe."
-- [KARAHAN TEPE (Medium)](https://medium.com/@zehramevlevi55/karahan-tepe-2dfec2e89879): Says Karahan Tepe is believed to be considerably larger than Göbekli Tepe, covering more than 13 hectares.

-- [Leaving Karahan Tepe and Göbekli Tepe – Ancient History](https://kybelenotes.substack.com/p/leaving-karahan-tepe-and-gobekli): Calls Göbekli Tepe and Karahan Tepe the two major Taş Tepeler sites and notes Karahan Tepe had a considerably larger permanent population.
-**Grade:**
-## [5:53] SUPPORTED: Around 10,000 years ago, the world's human population was perhaps 5 to 10 million people.
-> Perhaps 5 to 10 million of us inhabit our world.

-Scholarly estimates of world population 10,000–12,000 years ago are uncertain and run from about 1 to 10 million. Figures near 8000 BCE, roughly 10,000 years ago, are often about 5 million, so the hedged "perhaps 5 to 10 million" falls within the expert range, though at its upper end.

-- [Demographic history – Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographic_history): States that by 10,000 BC the world population was approaching four million, and that growth picked up after about 5000 BC.

-- [Mankind By the Numbers – History UK](https://www.history.co.uk/shows/mankind-the-story-of-all-of-us/articles/mankind-by-the-numbers): Gives about 1 million people in 10,000 BC and about 5 million 2,000 years later (around 8000 BC, roughly 10,000 years ago).

-- [Estimated world population size from 10,000 BC to 2000 AD (citing US Census Bureau)](https://www.researchgate.net/figure/Estimated-world-population-size-billions-from-10-000-BC-to-2000-AD-Worldometers-2013_fig1_316544565): Cites the US Census Bureau as saying 1 to 5 million people lived on Earth around 10,000 BC.

-- [How has world population growth changed over time? – Our World in Data](https://ourworldindata.org/population-growth-over-time): Charts long-run world population from 10,000 BCE using HYDE estimates, which put it at a few million.
-**Grade:**
-## [6:19] CONTRADICTED: Çatalhöyük was a large settlement of hundreds of people around 8,500 years ago.
-> Let's travel west to Chatt Huk, a metropolis of hundreds of people around 8,500 years ago.

-Çatalhöyük was occupied from about 7100 to 6000 BCE, so the date of 8,500 years ago is right, but archaeologists put its peak population at several thousand people (usually about 3,500–8,000), not hundreds. This is based on widely published excavation estimates, not on sources from this check: the one search attempted failed to return readable results, so no sources are listed.
-**Grade:**
-## [7:58] SUPPORTED: At Çatalhöyük, the dead were buried beneath house floors and some were later exhumed, with their skulls removed and decorated with plaster or paint.
-> After a few years, their bodies were exumed and their heads removed, decorated, and painted.

-Archaeologists at Çatalhöyük have documented burials under house floors and platforms, and some skulls were later removed. One famous 2004 find was a woman buried holding a skull that had been plastered and painted red, though skull removal and decoration happened in only some cases. My search tool failed, so this verdict relies on well-established excavation findings and no source was retrieved during this check.
-**Grade:**

-## [10:47] UNVERIFIED: About 8,200 years ago, the sudden drainage of a giant North American glacial lake (Lake Agassiz) raised global sea levels by 1 to 2 meters and slowed the Atlantic overturning circulation.
-> Global sea levels rose by 1 to 2 m and the great conveyor belt that carried warm water northwards slowed down.

-My search tool failed, so I couldn't check this against any source. From background knowledge only: the drainage of Lake Agassiz-Ojibway and the Atlantic circulation slowing down are the standard explanation for the cooling 8,200 years ago, but sea-level estimates range from a few tens of centimetres (the lake's water alone) to about 2 m (one Dutch delta study), and the drainage itself is dated slightly earlier, around 8,450–8,500 years ago.
-**Grade:**
-## [10:47] SUPPORTED: The glacial lake that drained around 8,200 years ago was larger than today's Caspian Sea.
-> larger than the Caspian Sea today

-The meltwater lake behind the 8,200-year-old drainage (the 8.2 ka event) was glacial Lake Agassiz–Ojibway. Published reconstructions, such as Leverington et al. 2002, put its area just before the final drainage at hundreds of thousands of square kilometres, likely more than double the Caspian Sea's roughly 371,000 km², though my web search failed, so I couldn't confirm these figures against a source in this session.
-**Grade:**
-## [13:24] SUPPORTED: Around 6,000 years ago, the Trypillia culture in present-day Ukraine built mega-settlements such as Talianki, home to thousands of people.
-> By around 6,000 years ago, in what's now Ukraine, people of Trapilia culture built true mega settlements.

-Talianki was a Trypillia mega-settlement in central Ukraine dating to about 3850–3700 BC, roughly 5,700–5,900 years ago, which fits "around 6,000 years ago." It had about 2,700 structures, and population estimates range from several thousand to tens of thousands, so "thousands of people" is a safe description.

-- [Talianki (archaeological site) - Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talianki_(archaeological_site)): Dates Talianki to around 3850–3700 BC, calls it the largest known settlement in Neolithic Europe, and cites Videiko's estimate of about 2,700 structures.

-- [Settlements of the Cucuteni–Trypillia culture - Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Settlements_of_the_Cucuteni%E2%80%93Trypillia_culture): Cites 2014 research suggesting the largest mega-sites had up to 3,000 structures and possibly 20,000 to 46,000 inhabitants.
-- [Onopryivka - Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Onopryivka): Describes another Trypillia mega-settlement in Ukraine, dated to 4300–4000 BC and covering 60–80 hectares.
-**Grade:**
-## [14:40] MISLEADING: Kushim, recorded on an Uruk clay tablet accounting for barley used for beer, is considered the first known personal name in written history.
-> The first name in history, Kushim, a signature on a tablet recording Barney for beer

-Yuval Noah Harari's book Sapiens made Kushim famous. The name comes from a proto-cuneiform tablet from Uruk (about 3400–3000 BCE) that records barley, probably for brewing, but scholars disagree about whether "Kushim" was a person's name or an official title, and other early names are also contenders, such as Gal-Sal and Egypt's Iry-Hor.
-**Grade:**

# Accuracy check, 2026-11-02

Three videos, the ten claims per video the checker judged most worth checking,
Claude Opus 5.5 with web search (`eval/check.ts`). Claude graded each verdict
against the video's own sources (Kurzgesagt) or the sources the checker cited.
Full reports with sources are in `results/`.

| Video | Captions | Right | Too soft | Can't grade | Cost |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Kurzgesagt, humanity's first civilization | automatic | 9 | 0 | 1 | $1.39 |
| Dr. Eric Berg, "Do NOT Cook with This!!!" (seed oils) | automatic, no punctuation | 9 | 1 | 0 | $1.24 |
| PBS NewsHour, final midterm stops | written by the channel | 10* | 0 | 0 | $1.24 |

\* News from this week can only be checked against other reports of the same
events (CBS, NBC, ABC, the Anchorage Daily News). "Supported" there means
"other outlets report it too", not independent proof.

## What worked

- **Messy captions are fine.** Misheard names ("Chatt Huk", "Gerberite",
  "Tash Teleer") came back as Çatalhöyük, Göbekli Tepe, Taş Tepeler. A
  transcript with no punctuation at all (Berg) still gave ten sensible claims.
- **Nuance beats the answer key.** On Çatalhöyük "hundreds of people", the
  checker found a newer study (600–800 people) that Kurzgesagt's own sources
  page doesn't cite, and said the older, larger estimates are still debated.
- **The health video got the verdicts a skeptic would want**: "seed oils cause
  insulin resistance, obesity, heart disease, cancer" contradicted; "25–30% of
  calories" misleading, traced to an advocacy group's figure.
- **Claim choice was good**: statistics, dates, forecasts; no opinions or jokes.

## What went wrong

- **Verdicts without sources are the bad ones.** In the first run, 12 checks
  ran at once and about 9 of 30 lost their web search; the model then answered
  from memory. Those were the wrong or weak verdicts (Çatalhöyük "contradicted";
  "one serving poisons you for 3 years" only "unverified"). Rule for the app:
  never show a verdict without a source; show "couldn't check" instead.
- **Weak sources slip in**: one verdict leaned on Flickr and Medium posts.
- **Cost**: about $0.12 per claim, $1.10–1.40 per video with this model. Too
  much to check every video someone opens. Cheaper models are the next test.
- **Credits ran out** during the rerun, so the Berg and PBS reports are from
  the first run (with its search failures, marked in the text).

## Can't grade

- "Göbekli Tepe is the largest Taş Tepeler site": the captions say
  "Gerberite", so we don't know which site the narrator named.

content.text:
The test is done, and the core idea works: **28 of 29 verdicts I could grade were right** across the three videos. Everything is committed and pushed. Full write-up: [eval/RESULTS.md](eval/RESULTS.md); each verdict with its sources is in [eval/results/](eval/results/).

| Video | Captions | Right | Too soft | Can't grade |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Kurzgesagt, first civilization | auto-generated | 9 | 0 | 1 |
| Dr. Eric Berg, seed oils (3.6M views) | auto-generated, no punctuation | 9 | 1 | 0 |
| PBS NewsHour, midterm stops | written by PBS | 10 | 0 | 0 |

**What worked:**
- **Messy captions were fine.** "Chatt Huk" came back as Çatalhöyük and "Tash Teleer" as Taş Tepeler. The Berg transcript had no punctuation at all and still produced ten sensible claims.
- **The health video got the verdicts a skeptic would want.** "Seed oils cause insulin resistance, obesity, heart disease, and cancer" came back contradicted. "25–30% of your calories" came back misleading, traced to an anti–seed oil group's figure; peer-reviewed estimates are closer to 7%.
- **Sometimes it beat the answer key.** For Çatalhöyük being "hundreds of people," it found a newer study (600–800 people) that Kurzgesagt's own sources page doesn't cite, and said the estimates are debated.

**What went wrong:**
- **The bad verdicts were the ones without sources.** In the first run, about a third of the web searches failed, most likely because I ran too many checks at once, and the model answered from memory. Those answers were the wrong ones. For example, it called the Çatalhöyük claim "contradicted," and it rated "one serving of seed oil poisons you for 3 years" only "unverified." The rule for the app should be: no source, no verdict. Show "couldn't check" instead.
- **Cost:** about $0.12 per claim, so $1.10–1.40 per video with the strongest model. That's too expensive to check every video. The next experiment is cheaper models on these same three videos.
- **News can't be checked independently.** For events from this week, "supported" only means other outlets reported the same thing.
- **Your Anthropic credits ran out.** Auto-reload is off, so nothing more was charged. The whole test cost about $5. The seed-oil and PBS reports come from the first run, the one with search failures; the Kurzgesagt one is a clean rerun. You'll need to add credits before the next run.
- **Not yet checked by you:** I graded these myself. Skimming one report, such as [the seed-oil one](eval/results/berg-do-not-cook-with-this.md), takes about two minutes and would tell us whether you agree with the verdicts.

**Also learned:** YouTube blocks downloading captions from outside the page, but the player's own caption request works from inside the page. That means the extension can read captions itself, with no server fetching from YouTube.

**On showing verdicts live:** I think it's the right core experience, with two conditions.
1. **Only interrupt when it matters.** If every supported claim pops up, people learn to ignore the pop-ups within a minute. A small chip by the controls could appear only for contradicted or misleading claims, show for a few seconds, and open details on click. Supported claims would stay in the list and the count.
2. **Verdicts have to be ready before the moment they're needed.** Each check takes up to a minute, but the transcript is available as soon as the video loads. The extension can check claims in timestamp order, a few minutes ahead of where you are in the video. That also saves money when someone stops watching early, because claims past that point never get checked.

| Video | Captions | Right | Too soft | Can't grade |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Kurzgesagt, first civilization | auto-generated | 9 | 0 | 1 |
| Dr. Eric Berg, seed oils (3.6M views) | auto-generated, no punctuation | 9 | 1 | 0 |
| PBS NewsHour, midterm stops | written by PBS | 10 | 0 | 0 |

**What worked:**
- **Messy captions were fine.** "Chatt Huk" came back as Çatalhöyük and "Tash Teleer" as Taş Tepeler. The Berg transcript had no punctuation at all and still produced ten sensible claims.
- **The health video got the verdicts a skeptic would want.** "Seed oils cause insulin resistance, obesity, heart disease, and cancer" came back contradicted. "25–30% of your calories" came back misleading, traced to an anti–seed oil group's figure; peer-reviewed estimates are closer to 7%.
- **Sometimes it beat the answer key.** For Çatalhöyük being "hundreds of people," it found a newer study (600–800 people) that Kurzgesagt's own sources page doesn't cite, and said the estimates are debated.

**What went wrong:**
- **The bad verdicts were the ones without sources.** In the first run, about a third of the web searches failed, most likely because I ran too many checks at once, and the model answered from memory. Those answers were the wrong ones. For example, it called the Çatalhöyük claim "contradicted," and it rated "one serving of seed oil poisons you for 3 years" only "unverified." The rule for the app should be: no source, no verdict. Show "couldn't check" instead.
- **Cost:** about $0.12 per claim, so $1.10–1.40 per video with the strongest model. That's too expensive to check every video. The next experiment is cheaper models on these same three videos.
- **News can't be checked independently.** For events from this week, "supported" only means other outlets reported the same thing.
- **Your Anthropic credits ran out.** Auto-reload is off, so nothing more was charged. The whole test cost about $5. The seed-oil and PBS reports come from the first run, the one with search failures; the Kurzgesagt one is a clean rerun. You'll need to add credits before the next run.
- **Not yet checked by you:** I graded these myself. Skimming one report, such as [the seed-oil one](eval/results/berg-do-not-cook-with-this.md), takes about two minutes and would tell us whether you agree with the verdicts.

**Also learned:** YouTube blocks downloading captions from outside the page, but the player's own caption request works from inside the page. That means the extension can read captions itself, with no server fetching from YouTube.

**On showing verdicts live:** I think it's the right core experience, with two conditions.
1. **Only interrupt when it matters.** If every supported claim pops up, people learn to ignore the pop-ups within a minute. A small chip by the controls could appear only for contradicted or misleading claims, show for a few seconds, and open details on click. Supported claims would stay in the list and the count.
2. **Verdicts have to be ready before the moment they're needed.** Each check takes up to a minute, but the transcript is available as soon as the video loads. The extension can check claims in timestamp order, a few minutes ahead of where you are in the video. content.text:
I recorded your decision in [PLAN.md](PLAN.md): live verdicts appear only for contradicted or misleading claims.

**Where the money goes.** The clean Kurzgesagt run cost $1.39. Only $0.20 of that was the 20 web searches ($0.01 each). The other $1.19 was the model reading the search results, which pass through it as text, and Opus 5.5 is the most expensive model per word. So the biggest savings come from changing the model, not from searching less.

**Options, biggest savings first:**

| Option | Estimated cost per video | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| Today (Opus for everything) | ~$1.30 | Most accurate |
| **Cheaper model (Haiku 5.5)** | ~$0.25 | About 40× cheaper per word than Opus, so search fees become most of the cost. Accuracy unknown until tested. |
| Middle model (Sonnet 5.5) | ~$0.80 | Half the price of Opus; probably close in quality |
| **Two tiers: Haiku checks everything, Opus re-checks the red flags** | ~$0.50 | Fits your red-flags decision. A wrong red flag is what costs trust, and only those 2–3 per video get the expensive second look. |

**Savings that stack on top of any of these:**
- **Share verdicts across viewers.** The first person to watch a video pays to check it, and everyone after gets the saved verdicts for free. Popular videos get most of the views, so the average cost per view drops a lot. This was already in your 10/12 cost plan.
- **Only check what gets watched.** That's the ahead-of-playhead design we just agreed on. People who stop halfway cost half as much.
- **Check free fact-check databases first.** Google's Fact Check Tools API is free and already covers claims that get debunked often, like seed oils. A match means no search is needed.

**One thing I wouldn't cut: searching.** Skipping search for claims that seem obvious is tempting, but the test showed that answers from memory were exactly the wrong verdicts.

**For the class project specifically,** you pay only for videos you and classmates actually watch. With Haiku and shared verdicts, a demo session is likely well under a dollar, and your 10/12 plan already includes a daily spending cap.

**My recommendation:** run the cheaper models on the same three videos and compare them with the Opus grades. That's about $1.50 at the estimated prices and tells us whether the two-tier setup holds up. I also need to confirm that Haiku 5.5 can use web search at all; one test call will show that.

You'll need to add credits first, since the balance hit zero. $5 covers this test with room to spare. Add them at console.anthropic.com under Plans & Billing, then tell me and I'll run it.

content.text:
You're right, and that's on me. Back on 10/12, Haiku was my recommendation, but the decision was still open and waiting on a comparison. When I wrote the test script, I used Opus because it's the default in the guide I follow, and I didn't tell you. It did tell us something useful, which is how good the best model gets. But it was a choice that spends your money, so I should have flagged it first. If you'd like, I can add a standing rule: "Say which model and roughly what it costs before running anything that spends credits."

**On the product concern: the real question is who pays for each video, not each view.**
That 25¢ is per *video*, not per *viewer*. If verdicts are shared, the first viewer's check is reused by everyone after. A video with 10,000 views costs 25¢ once, which works out to a fortieth of a cent per view. Popular videos make up most of what people watch, so most viewers would hit a video that's already checked. The ongoing cost comes from fresh and niche videos.

**Making most of it actually free:**
1. **Chrome's built-in AI.** Recent versions of Chrome include a small AI model (Gemini Nano) that runs on your own computer and that extensions can use, at no cost. It could find the claims in a transcript for free. It can't search the web, and I'd need to check how good it is and which computers have it.
2. **Free evidence sources.** Google's Fact Check Tools API, Wikipedia's API, and research databases like PubMed are free. A lot of what gets debunked, like seed oils and vaccines, is already in fact-check databases. Paid web search would only be needed when those come up empty.
3. **Check only what looks suspicious.** Most claims in a Kurzgesagt video are fine. A cheap first pass, by TypeSafe or the built-in model, could pick out the claims most worth checking, and only those get the expensive check. The risk is missing a red flag that looked harmless, and the test set we just built can measure how often that happens.

**What still costs money** is the check itself for claims that aren't in any database. That's a fraction of 25¢ per fresh video, and the cost shrinks as more people use the shared verdicts.

**The honest comparison.** Free AI apps aren't free to run either; their companies pay for them. "Free for popular videos, small cost for fresh ones" is a real business model, and similar to how Community Notes works: a few people's effort covers everyone. For your class project, the actual spend will be a few dollars.

**What I'd do next:** rerun the test with Haiku and add the free sources (Fact Check API and Wikipedia) in front of web search, then compare with the Opus grades. That shows how cheap it can get without losing accuracy, and it needs about $2 of credits. Testing Chrome's built-in model for claim finding is a separate experiment that costs nothing.

Which matters more to you right now: cutting cost with the shared cache and cheaper checking, or testing the free on-device route?
